clinicalPearls: A rare four-repeat tauopathy defined by globular tau-positive inclusions in oligodendrocytes and astrocytes rather than the neuronal tangles typical of other tauopathies
Clinical presentations are heterogeneous and may resemble behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia, corticobasal syndrome or a motor neurone disease-like syndrome with upper motor neurone signs
Frontotemporal atrophy with prominent white matter degeneration and corticospinal tract involvement is characteristic pathologically
The globular glial inclusions include distinctive globular oligodendroglial and astroglial tau aggregates that give the disorder its name
It is classified into subtypes reflecting the relative distribution of frontotemporal and motor pathology
There is no reliable biomarker in life, and diagnosis is confirmed neuropathologically
It should be considered within the differential of frontotemporal lobar degeneration syndromes, particularly when pyramidal signs accompany cognitive or behavioural change
reference.pathophysiology: Globular glial tauopathy is a form of frontotemporal lobar degeneration in the four-repeat tauopathy family, distinguished by the accumulation of abnormal tau as globular inclusions predominantly within glial cells, namely globular oligodendroglial inclusions and globular astrocytic inclusions, with comparatively less neuronal tau pathology. The disease affects frontotemporal cortex, subcortical white matter and, in many cases, the corticospinal tracts, which explains the frequent combination of behavioural, cognitive and pyramidal motor features. Progressive glial tau deposition and associated white matter degeneration underlie the clinical syndromes, which overlap with other frontotemporal and motor neurone disease presentations.
additionalDifferentials: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and motor neurone disease with cognitive involvement
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain to assess frontotemporal atrophy and white matter change
FDG-PET to characterise the pattern of cortical hypometabolism
Electromyography where a motor neurone disease-like syndrome is suspected
Amyloid PET or cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers to help exclude Alzheimer pathology
Neuropsychological assessment to define the cognitive and behavioural profile
redFlags: Emergence of upper motor neurone signs or bulbar involvement indicating a motor neurone disease-like course
Dysphagia with aspiration risk as motor features advance
reference.prognosis: Globular glial tauopathy is progressive, with the tempo and disability influenced by the balance of frontotemporal and motor involvement; those with prominent corticospinal or motor neurone-like features may decline more rapidly, and management is supportive and multidisciplinary.
pitfalls: Failing to consider a glial tauopathy when pyramidal signs accompany a frontotemporal syndrome
Assuming an Alzheimer or purely neuronal tauopathy substrate without neuropathological confirmation
Overlooking the motor neurone disease-like subtype in the differential of upper motor neurone syndromes
Expecting a specific in-life biomarker when diagnosis remains largely post-mortem
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: No disease-modifying therapy exists, so management is supportive and directed at the behavioural, cognitive and motor manifestations
Symptomatic treatment of behavioural and psychological features, with antispasticity measures for pyramidal upper motor neurone signs
Physiotherapy and occupational therapy to maintain mobility and function, with appropriate aids and falls prevention
Speech and language therapy for dysarthria and dysphagia, with nutritional support and consideration of enteral feeding as swallowing fails
Respiratory and secretion management where a motor neurone disease-like syndrome develops
Coordinate multidisciplinary care with cognitive neurology, neuropsychology and carer support, with early palliative involvement and advance care planning
